National Assembly
Twenty-first Session
Complete Details of Proceedings
Baisakh 28, 2083
Monday
Meeting Number - 1
The first meeting of the Twenty-first Session of the National Assembly commenced at 14:05 hours under the chairmanship of the Honourable Chairperson, Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal.
(14:05 hrs)
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable members, the proceedings of the first meeting of the Twenty-first Session of the Assembly will now commence. I warmly welcome all the Honourable members. Honourable members, a letter regarding the summoning of the session has been received from the Honourable President. I shall now inform you of the contents of the said letter.
To,
The Honourable Chairperson,
National Assembly,
Singh Durbar, Kathmandu.
As per Article 93, Sub-section (1) of the Constitution of Nepal, I, the President of Nepal, have summoned the joint session of the Federal Parliament to convene on Monday, Baisakh 28, 2083, at 14:00 hours in the Federal Parliament Building, Singh Durbar, on the recommendation of the Government of Nepal, Council of Ministers, dated Baisakh 22, 2083. (Ram Chandra Poudel) President, Baisakh 22, 2083.
Honourable members, let us now observe one minute of silence standing in tribute to the unknown martyrs who sacrificed their lives for democracy.
"Begin"
(Silence)
"Thank you"
Honourable members, we are gathered here today at the commencement of the 21st Session of the Federal Parliament, National Assembly, in continuation of the parliamentary democratic republican system established by the Constitution of 2072, which was built after the long sacrifices of the people. I heartily welcome all Honourable members on the occasion of the commencement of the 21st Session. I also extend my best wishes for the grand success of this session. The active participation, cooperation, sense of responsibility, and responsible role played by all of you in past sessions have established the National Assembly as a mature, stable, and guardian-like house. I express my heartfelt respect and gratitude to all Honourable members for this contribution. Even in difficult circumstances following the Gen-Z movement during the 18th session, the National Assembly conducted the 19th session, continuing parliamentary activities and advancing the legislative process. The general election was completed on Falgun 21st, a new government was formed, and the 20th session of the Federal Parliament was also completed. After the election, the Federal Parliament has gained completeness, and it is felt that parliamentary activities have gained momentum. These achievements have contributed to making the parliament accountable, transparent, and effective to the people. However, challenges such as the continuity of legislation, session schedules, building construction, and technical difficulties still remain before us. The new mandate passed by the House of Representatives has reaffirmed the supremacy of the people in the democratic system. The people have great expectations for good governance, transparency, service delivery, and development to gain momentum with the new government. In this situation, the National Assembly assures its support and cooperation for all constructive and positive actions of the government. It is hoped that the under-construction parliament building will be completed soon, and the assembly will be conducted in the new building with the use of modern technology, which will certainly enhance efficiency and transparency. From Baisakh 2 to 6, I, along with Honourable Member Krishna Bahadur Rokaya and Honourable Member Dr. Anjan Shakya from the National Assembly, participated as a Nepali parliamentary delegation in the 152nd General Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union held in Istanbul, Turkey. In the IPU General Assembly, on behalf of Nepal, I addressed the issues of the sense of hope, assurance of peace, and justice for future generations, expressing our views on the actions and roles we need to take to ensure peace, security, prosperity, human dignity, and sustainability in the world and bring about concrete and positive changes in people's lives. Additionally, a delegation of the Secretary and officials from the National Assembly, led by the Secretary-General, participated in the assembly. In the same program, I addressed the role of parliaments in ensuring adaptive urbanization in the context of climate change on behalf of Nepal. Similarly, courtesy calls were made with parliamentary delegations from countries including Turkey, China, Australia, and Bhutan. It is felt that this has played a specific role in expanding international cooperation, parliamentary collaboration, and diplomatic relations. The entire team feels that our presence and participation in that assembly were fruitful. Honourable members, this 21st session is the budget session. There will be in-depth discussions on the government's policy and program, the appropriation bill, and the budget. We have the responsibility to prioritize and pass bills such as the Federal Civil Service, School Education, and Nepal Police. In the meantime, there will also be in-depth discussions on the ordinances brought by the government and the bills replacing them. From this session onwards, we have also started the provision of sign language in the live broadcast of parliamentary meetings as stipulated in the National Assembly Rules of Procedure, 2075. Starting today. In the past, due to the inability to maintain the continuity of legislation, important legislative bills were rendered ineffective, failing to address the immediate needs of the country. The parliament's efficiency can be increased only through scheduled meetings, timely introduction of bills, active committees, and government cooperation. Our common objective is the welfare, prosperity, and good governance of the people. To achieve this goal, it is necessary today to rise above political differences, prejudices, and biases and prioritize national interests. I am confident that we will participate seriously throughout this session, rising above party interests and prioritizing the nation's needs. Expressing confidence in your active participation in the dignified role of the assembly, the support of the secretariat, and the cooperation of the government, I wish the 21st session complete success. Thank you. Honourable members, in the context of the commencement of the Twenty-first Session of the National Assembly, names have been received to present their views on behalf of the parties represented in the National Assembly. I will now provide time to the Honourable members sequentially. First, Honourable Member Kamala Panta. Honourable Mr. Kamala Panta (Nepali Congress): Honourable Chairperson, just a moment ago, we observed one minute of silence and paid tribute to the martyrs. Respecting the honourable elders, Chairperson, we have entered the 21st session, which is the first budget session after the general election held on Falgun 21st. Naturally, we are surrounded by the countless aspirations of the people at this moment. The people, through their votes, have clearly expressed their desire for political stability and rapid economic development. Honourable Chairperson, looking at the activities and style of work of the government in its initial days, I must sadly state that this government appears arbitrary, autocratic, and insensitive towards the helpless and the poor in terms of setting priorities for its work and its governance mentality. Chairperson, the election was for the House of Representatives. The House of Representatives exercised its constitutional authority and formed a new government, but unfortunately, this very parliament came under the first attack from the government. The scheduled meeting of the parliament was suddenly adjourned without any reason or basis. A flood of ordinances was issued with the intention of weakening the special privilege of the parliament to enact laws. The government's behavior has been deceptive even in completing the budget statement. Honourable Chairperson, I caution the government, which argues that it is taking unconventional paths to accomplish much in a short time, not to jump from the balcony of the upper floor if it needs to reach the ground quickly. The government's means or tools of governance is the constitution of the country. We have reached this parliament through the constitution and in a constitutional manner. The constitution and prevailing laws are the basis for solutions rooted in compassion, love, trust, and faith in the people. Honourable Chairperson, we feel that the government is currently misusing its authority. Even while expressing goodwill and stating that we are here to support the government, our duty is to protect the constitution. I feel that this government has made a mockery of the constitution. However, the current government is using state terror as a tool of governance. There is state terror now. In such a short time! This chain of governance terror, which began with the insult and degradation of the civil administration, has left thousands of landless squatters homeless. Countless elderly mothers and fathers, and innocent children have been thrown into disarray. Their present and future have been looted by their own guardians. Honourable Chairperson, the state, as a guardian, is a guardian of every citizen. We have a constitution that was built through long struggles, starting from 2007, by parties that have been named as old and continuously struggling. When we said that no one is above the constitution, the government has been working above the constitution. The leadership should not be left without leadership for a few days. Various universities, the Health University, health institutes, constitutional bodies, and organizations have been kept without proper alternative arrangements. The current government, which came to power as an alternative to the previous government with the slogan of change, has shown its prowess by surpassing even old manipulations in the Constitutional Council's procedures through ordinances in its very first move. It has become clear that it is attacking the dignity, respect, and trustworthy continuity of the Supreme Court, which has remained intact until today. This has sown the seeds of a far-reaching wrong practice in the impartial and clean sky of the Nepali judiciary. Chairperson, the Honourable Prime Minister, who once appeared very sensitive about an incident involving his wife and wrote various things on social media, has now demonstrated the arrogance of majority against capable women, which has hurt the feelings of women in general. We women are hurt. An attack has been made on a senior woman Chief Justice, who has been running the judiciary, solely because she is a woman. It is the general perception that this is heinous violence against women carried out with the backing of ordinances and the judiciary. The government's view of the Free Student Union is itself flawed. Honourable Chairperson, the Free Student Union is flawed. We cannot forget the contribution of conscious youth students to the open competitive political system we are in today. The understanding that students of the past only engaged in vandalism and violence, and only gave rise to distortions, and that student unions and organizations are wrong, is itself wrong. It should not be forgotten that those who consider themselves superior today have themselves passed through the doors of these colleges and universities. The talent and competence of today's capable administrators, strong human resources, and visionary leaders were all nurtured there. If the water is polluted, should we clean it or destroy the source? Trade union rights are not subject to the government's discretion. It is considered the backbone of a democratic governance system. As a member state of the International Labour Organization, we cannot shy away from international competition. The government's strong undemocratic intention is evident in its attempt to suppress trade unions instead of discussing how they can be made more organized, disciplined, and focused on professional rights and welfare. The government should correct itself in time; there is time, the government should correct itself; democratic methods and procedures.

With the utmost respect for parliamentary sanctity, may the government be serious about fulfilling public aspirations. Honorable Chairperson, Sir, best wishes, and let it be known that we have come this far through student struggles. Student organizations have benefited the country. Thank you.

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Jhaku Prasad Subedi.

(14:22 hrs)

Honorable Mr. Jhaku Prasad Subedi (Nepal Communist Party): Honorable Chairperson,

(14:23 hrs)

Sir, first of all, I want to extend my best wishes for the success of this ongoing session. May a proper budget and proper policies and programs be introduced. This will surely make the success of this session meaningful. But the issue that needs to be raised here is something we all know. After the President summoned the parliament, the government, on the recommendation of the government, postponed the meeting without it even commencing, and ordinances were suddenly introduced. These are very serious matters. This practice is contrary to democratic values and principles and the tradition of a multi-party political system. The government has devalued parliamentary sanctity. The government's process of bringing ordinances by circumventing the parliament appears to be against democracy. The government, which came to power with the support of nearly a two-thirds majority and with the slogan of change, resorting to ordinances on serious matters is a new development in Nepali politics.

Honorable Chairperson, Sir, Article 114 of the Constitution envisions ordinances only when immediate action is necessary. Parliament is the supreme forum for national debate and accountability. The government must understand this very seriously. Circumventing parliament is an insult to the collective wisdom of the elected representatives. It is a disregard for the rule of law. This government is not only making a mockery of parliament but also attempting to undermine democracy. For a majority government to rule through ordinances is a threat to democracy and an attempt to turn the rule of law into autocratic rule.

Chairperson, Sir, making decisions through ordinances by adjourning parliament is not just a procedural matter; it raises questions about the government's intentions. The government has misused power, believing that power is everything and that constitution and law are nothing. The government talks about good governance. What is good governance? Good governance means respecting the sanctity of the constitution and law. This ordinance was brought with the intention of appointing one's own people to constitutional bodies. The government must first understand the separation of powers very seriously. The government is meant to lead the executive, but these ordinances suggest that the government also wants to lead the judiciary and the legislature. These ordinances have been brought with that intention. The government has challenged the separation of powers. Looking at the ordinances related to the Constitutional Council and the removal of office-bearers, it appears purely motivated by political self-interest, which has already become evident in the appointment of Supreme Court judges or in those decisions. The ordinance states that three members, including the Prime Minister, must be present for a majority in the six-member Constitutional Council. How can three members constitute a majority in a six-member Constitutional Council? A majority requires a supermajority, doesn't it? The Supreme Court interpreted that 39 members would be a majority in the 60-member Gandaki Provincial Assembly. How can three members, including the Prime Minister, constitute a majority in the six-member Constitutional Council for the appointment of the Chief Justice? Honorable Chairperson, Sir, this ordinance is against democracy, constitutional values, and traditions. May the government not repeat such mistakes.

Chairperson, Sir, that's not all. Regarding the government's mistakes, during the elections, the top leader of Rastriya Swatantra Party, while asking for votes in the squatter settlements, said that if the government bulldozed them, he would stand in front of them with his chest. Currently, bulldozers are running over the squatter settlements. You have committed a great political betrayal against the squatters.

The plight of the squatters was pitiful. The capitalist class has displaced the working class. Where is the real identification of the squatters? Why is force being used without providing alternative arrangements? Squatters cannot even live by the riverbanks or in difficult places. Who would want to live in such places, Honorable Chairperson, Sir? That is a compulsion. The government used bulldozers to oppress the poor and the helpless, created terror with the force of guns, and displaced even those who had no other homes. This government has committed a crime against humanity. Even a criminal is asked about their last wish before being given the death penalty. But the government did not listen to the suffering of the squatters; it reveled in oppressing them. The government says it is its job to protect public land, Chairperson, Sir. Then whose job is it to manage the squatters? Who will take responsibility for the body of Rabin Lama found in Balkhu River? Who was responsible for saving the life of Indrabahadur Rai, who committed suicide, Chairperson? The government has caused misery to women, the disabled, pregnant women, the sick, the elderly, and students. They could not bear the pain and committed suicide. The main issue now is the removal of squatters without management, Honorable Prime Minister, you say you want to see the country smile. Prime Minister, will the country smile if you make millions of squatters across the country cry? Thank you.

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Prem Prasad Dangal.

(14:31 hrs)

Honorable Mr. Prem Prasad Dangal (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honorable

(14:32 hrs)

Chairperson, Sir, today we are participating in the first meeting of the 21st session. Our collective aspiration is to eradicate economic inequality from our country and achieve sustainable peace, development, and prosperity. We will succeed in that. For this, may we be able to do some meaningful work through this session, and may the policies, programs, and budget brought by the Government of Nepal also be oriented towards this direction. We all have a role to play. I extend my heartfelt best wishes to all the honorable members for this.

Honorable Chairperson, Sir, now I would like to present some views from my party's perspective regarding some of the government's activities. Regarding the ordinances, the previous honorable members have already raised the issue. According to Article 124 of the Constitution, except when the sessions of both houses of the Federal Parliament are in progress, in other situations where immediate action is necessary, such as civil war, war, or natural disaster, severe natural disaster, epidemic, when parliament cannot be convened immediately, and laws cannot be made. In such times, if something needs to be done, the government can bring an ordinance, and the President can issue an ordinance upon the recommendation of the Council of Ministers. However, this has been severely misused during this period. The Government of Nepal has brought 8 different ordinances, including an amendment to the Act relating to the functions, duties, and powers of the Constitutional Council. I do not want to go into the details of those ordinances. 8 ordinances have been brought. When a party with nearly a two-thirds majority in the House of Representatives leads the government, laws can be made as the ruling party desires. If there was a genuine desire to work, the process could have been expedited. I do not want to go into the details. The law and rules give the authority to expedite the process in the parliament and make laws. Despite this, the parliament was convened and then suddenly adjourned, and ordinances were brought by circumventing parliament. Not a single bill was presented in parliament. Parliament convened multiple times, but not a single bill was presented. Parliament could not make a single law during this period, but bringing ordinances one after another is a highly undemocratic and unparliamentary move. We strongly oppose this. It is regrettable that the government has started the law-making process through ordinances. The government has initiated the process of bringing laws through ordinances. From my party's perspective, I strongly oppose and condemn this move. I demand that the Government of Nepal immediately repeal these ordinances. Otherwise, we will act according to the powers granted to the National Assembly by law and rules. We will do what we have to do. I wish to submit this.

Honorable Chairperson, Sir, now I would like to say something regarding the appointment of the Chief Justice. Article 284 of the Constitution of Nepal provides for the Constitutional Council. I do not want to go into detail here. The Council appoints the heads and officials of constitutional bodies. This arrangement ensures representation from the main bodies of the state – the executive, legislature, and judiciary – in the Council. It also includes the leader of the opposition party. The main purpose of this is to ensure that officials of constitutional bodies are appointed based on the principle of separation of powers. This provision has been made to ensure participation from all aspects of the state based on the separation of powers, to create a sense of ownership, and political ownership. Constitutional bodies should not be controlled by the state. The constitution has made provisions for appointments and functions and duties so that the government cannot change constitutional bodies according to its interests to curb the oversight of the government. The government has brought ordinances to ensure decisions in its favor, and this is wrong. This is also wrong according to the verdict and interpretation of the Supreme Court on 2081/02/14. We all must abide by this. In the six-member Constitutional Council, three members cannot form a majority. According to the Supreme Court's interpretation, there is an established judicial process and practice for the appointment of the Chief Justice in our country. The established judicial tradition of the senior-most judge becoming the Chief Justice in Nepal's 80-year judicial history has been violated without basis or reason. We strongly oppose this.

Honorable Chairperson, Sir, now I would like to briefly address the ordinances related to the removal of public office-bearers. It is a matter of great objection that the appointment of office-bearers involved in the selection process, including the Chairperson and members of the Public Service Commission, based on specific acts, rules, laws, procedures, directives, and decisions, is being called politicization. These office-bearers have been recruited and appointed to their respective bodies according to specific acts, rules, and laws. However, by removing these office-bearers and appointing others through the same acts, rules, laws, and procedures, the ruling party is politicizing them. In reality, governments and coalitions have been formed multiple times in the past, but now a single ruling party is forming a single government and is politicizing it. This is something we are experiencing. Some bodies have been formed by bringing special acts, and the appointments and recruitments of those officials have been made accordingly. Those laws are special laws. Ordinances are treated as ordinary laws. However, ordinances cannot be used to control special laws by treating them as ordinary laws. Special laws had defined the tenure of office-bearers, but the ordinance has removed the tenure and left it to the government's discretion. We object to such arbitrary actions.

Honorable Chairperson, Sir, now I would like to briefly express my views on some current issues. The work of evicting settlements in various places across the country, including the Kathmandu Valley, without collecting identity information, conducting investigations, and verification of unregistered residents, and without ensuring alternative housing, has been intensified. This has drawn our serious attention, and we oppose it. We oppose this action of the government.

I express my objection to the attitude, I protest. In this situation, citizens living in such settlements are experiencing widespread insecurity and fear. In this, especially children, pregnant women, new mothers, senior citizens, and families in distress are more affected. Two landless citizens have committed suicide. Who will take responsibility for this? Another question arises: who will take responsibility for this? The government must take responsibility. I want to state this. The constitution guarantees the right to housing for Nepali citizens. I strongly urge the Nepal government to immediately arrange safe housing and provide a long-term solution to this problem, considering the livelihoods, health risks, and other issues of all landless citizens, without investigating, collecting data, identifying, and verifying landless and unmanaged settlers, and without ensuring alternative housing.

There has been a sharp increase in the prices of daily necessities such as lentils, rice, vegetables, fruits, spices, and other kitchen ingredients. Inflation has skyrocketed. Therefore, I sincerely request that inflation and black marketing be controlled immediately, and relief be provided to citizens by establishing a public distribution system and operating fair-price shops for the poor, laborers, farmers, and marginalized communities.

Similarly, the public is suffering due to the repeated sharp increases in the prices of petroleum products. I draw the attention of the state to immediately announce relief packages to address the price hike in petroleum products by streamlining the supply chain and strictly monitoring the market to provide relief to consumers.

Finally, my request is that the government has been taking actions such as dissolving, banning, and controlling various associations and organizations. The government has directly violated the fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by the constitution to citizens. Students, laborers, and professionals have been deprived of their right to form organizations, become members, and advocate for their professional, community, and class rights and interests. The state, this government, has stifled these rights.

By restricting the right to organize, which is guaranteed by democracy, the government is moving towards authoritarianism. These actions of the government are unconstitutional. Therefore, I strongly demand that the ordinances brought to dissolve student, labor, and civil servant organizations be immediately repealed.

Thank you. Namaste.

Honorable Chairperson: - Honorable Member Mahanta Thakur.
(14:43 hrs)
Honorable Mr. Mahanta Thakur (Democratic Socialist Party, Nepal): - Thank you, Honorable Chairperson, for giving me time, and best wishes to you as well. I will only take two or four minutes. We are very happy that we have got a new Madhesh Province. You might know too. That Kalapani, Lipulekh, Limpiyadhura. But we haven't gone to that place. I hear a lot about 'dal-dal' (muddy areas/parties). If we go, we'll get stuck. That's why we haven't gone yet. If the government gives us an opportunity sometime, we will go, happily. Because the old Madhesh Province, that is a province outside our border. But it is Nepali, we accept it as Nepali. It is a province of Nepalis, outside our border. The movement we had undertaken. The agendas we had put forth in that movement were to remove the discrimination that has been happening from the beginning based on caste, religion, region, labor, etc. Discrimination has been happening since ancient times. How to remove it? The federal system that was brought based on the basis of what kind of needs, what basis, and what was envisioned for the country was that based on caste and religion, wherever there is a larger population, it should be according to that, and a committee was also formed for that. First, the committee went province-wise in 16 Madhesh. Then there were 10/11, and it was somewhat acceptable to us. The imagination of two Madhesh provinces, east and west. We thought it was fine. One was the Jhapa group, and the other was from the east up to Jhapa. Then we had accepted it as Tharuhat in the western Madhesh, from that. But that also didn't happen. And the current seven provinces are... That's why, as soon as we hear the name of the constitution, in our minds, in our senses, any constitution will be made, is being made, or will be amended. Now, things are happening haphazardly. The parliament was convened, opened, and then closed. After closing, ordinances have been brought. Now, what kind of ordinances will they be? In any case, if we are not satisfied with the constitution itself. Then how can we accept such ordinances? We will not accept what it says in any way. Secondly, as you have seen, although it might be due to age, I have difficulty walking around. Even when going up the stairs, the attendant helped me get here. Even in that condition, I tell the public and myself one thing: the head of our current government, you are the Prime Minister. The head of the government, he has come to the area from which I come. Mahottari's constituency number three. He didn't win in one of them, which is this area. Madhesh is already in ruins, and I have tried to talk to ministers many times before about its development. I also wanted to meet them and requested them to meet me, Prime Minister. Write my name to your secretary. I will meet you. I know you, I will meet you. Since we are from the same place, you know me. Since you are from my own place, there is a little affection too. We thought that since there is a Madhesi Prime Minister, he would not discriminate against Madhesis, and we would not be beaten. Now, they have emptied all the party offices. The government is going to seize them. But my photo has been taken, and this is the Madhesi party office, how can they remove it? Perhaps they might break the furniture inside or move it. It hasn't been moved, but the thought is there, maybe move the furniture elsewhere. Who knows, I have to deal with such mad people. At any time, they can do anything. Now, I don't speak as sweetly as you do. I have become so hardened from enduring so much. My body also doesn't work. I might faint and fall while walking. That's the condition. Still, I am able to be present among you, and as long as I am able, in whatever condition, I will be with you. I will support you. Saying this, I once again thank the Chairperson very much and extend my best wishes. But after this work, there will be no good wishes.

Honorable Chairperson: - Honorable Member Tul Prasad Bishwakarma
(14:50 hrs)
Honorable Mr. Tul Prasad Bishwakarma (National People's Front): - Honorable Chairperson,
First of all, I wish the upcoming session success and urge the current government to proceed with its work in accordance with the wishes and desires of the country and the people. However, the events that have occurred in the country during this period have raised questions about the government's actions. Here, landless people have been displaced. It is extremely wrong to evict people from their residences just as the monsoon is about to begin, without proper management for many, and the government has acted extremely cruelly. Similarly, we are seeing that the government itself recommended convening the session and then postponed it again, bringing eight ordinances. And looking at those ordinances, it is generally understood that those ordinances have not been brought with good intentions. Therefore, regarding the things that have come in those ordinances, to put it broadly, as other honorable speakers mentioned earlier, how can there be a majority of 3 out of a committee of 6? It is a tradition and recognition of the world that a majority requires 51 percent of the vote. But 3 out of 6 votes is only 50 percent. So, what is this government trying to do? We can definitely infer. Therefore, these ordinances, with the intentions with which they have been brought, will not benefit the people and the nation. They cannot uphold the spirit of the constitution. Therefore, I want to state here that the government must back down from these ordinances.

Similarly, various incidents have occurred in the country during this period. Professional organizations, student organizations, trade unions, and other professional organizations have been dissolved and banned. This is contrary to democratic values, norms, and the spirit of the constitution of a federal Nepal. Therefore, I urge the government to withdraw its decision. Because in any democratic country, its citizens have the right to organize for their professional dignity and their professional rights and progress, and they have the status to present their demands to the government.

Similarly, during this period, oppression against the Dalit community has increased significantly. Incidents of murder and violence against Dalit men and women are repeatedly occurring in various parts of the country. For a long time, we have repeatedly raised the issue of the upliftment of Dalits, the protection of their lives, and the assurance of their rights and interests in the parliament. However, the government, which came with promises, and apologized for the injustices against Dalits, has not shown that in practice today. In Inisa BK, she was murdered through gang rape; in Sindhuli, a Dalit youth died in custody due to extreme torture simply for inter-caste marriage, and such incidents have occurred elsewhere. And in Rolpa, a Dalit minor was beaten to near death on the charge of entering a house. Therefore, the government should take responsible steps to prevent such incidents.

I make this demand to the government through this parliament, through the Honorable Chairperson. Therefore, today we hoped that this country would change. This government, with a two-thirds majority, would give the country a new destination. But looking at the activities so far, this government is continuously moving on the path of authoritarianism. Therefore, if the authoritarian character of this government does not change, the people will have to rise from the streets against this government one day. I want to say that such a situation does not arise and the government should be alert in time, and with this, I conclude my brief remarks. Thank you.

Adjournment: 14:02 hrs.
The National Assembly meeting, which was adjourned for 10 minutes today, resumed under the chairmanship of the Honourable Chairperson, Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal, at 15:14 hrs.
96
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Members, the proceedings of the National Assembly meeting, which was adjourned for 10 minutes today,
(15:14 hrs.)
commence now. Honourable Members, I now provide the floor to the Honourable Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Sobita Gautam, on behalf of the Honourable Prime Minister, Sher Bahadur Deuba, to present the Public Procurement (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 2083, the Ordinance Relating to the Removal of Public Office Holders, 2083, and the Constitutional Council (Functions, Duties, Powers and Procedures) (First Amendment) Ordinance, 2083 before the House.
Honourable Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Ms. Sobita Gautam:-
(14:05 hrs.)
Honourable Chairperson, to ensure greater competition and transparency in the procedures and decisions related to public procurement, to promote integrity and accountability, to achieve maximum returns from public expenditure in a frugal and judicious manner, and to enhance the management capacity of public bodies in procuring goods, consulting services, and other services for construction works, and to ensure equal opportunities for producers, sellers, suppliers, construction entrepreneurs, or service providers to participate in the public procurement process without discrimination, and to guarantee good governance, it is necessary to amend the existing provisions of the Public Procurement Act. Therefore, the Public Procurement (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 2083 has been promulgated. This ordinance significantly reduces the timelines from the invitation of bids to other deadlines, keeping in mind the time required to operate and complete projects. A flexible arrangement has been made to procure essential and sensitive goods such as fertilizer, medicine, and information technology through special procedures. Provisions such as prioritizing the procurement of domestic goods, implementing the concept of e-marketplace to reduce public expenditure, and making the authority to issue variation orders accountable have been included. Therefore, with the permission of the Honourable Chairperson, I present the Public Procurement (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 2083, promulgated under Article 114 (1) of the Constitution of Nepal, before the esteemed House. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson, with the objective of immediately enacting legal provisions regarding the removal of public office holders appointed, nominated, or designated under existing laws, and to completely displace old appointments made before Chaitra 12, 2082, in public bodies, regardless of any terms, facilities, or tenure specified, and to initiate new appointments from scratch based on a merit system, and to make future appointed office holders fully accountable for their responsibilities, it is necessary to immediately amend the relevant provisions in the Act. Therefore, with the permission of the Honourable Chairperson, I present the Ordinance Relating to the Removal of Public Office Holders, 2083, promulgated under Article 114 (1) of the Constitution of Nepal, before the esteemed House. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson, the Constitutional Council (Functions, Duties, Powers and Procedures) Act, 2066 is in implementation to regulate the functions, duties, and powers of the Constitutional Council. It has become necessary to immediately amend the provisions of the said Act, hence the Constitutional Council (Functions, Duties, Powers and Procedures) (First Amendment) Ordinance, 2083 has been promulgated. In this ordinance, to manage the time and prioritize the decision-making process of the Council meetings, and to address the situation where meetings are repeatedly adjourned due to lack of quorum, the quorum has been adjusted in proportion to the number of members present, ensuring that meetings can be conducted continuously. Therefore, with the permission of the Honourable Chairperson, I present the Constitutional Council (Functions, Duties, Powers and Procedures) (First Amendment) Ordinance, 2083, promulgated under Article 114 (1) of the Constitution of Nepal, before the esteemed House. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Members, I now provide the floor to the Honourable Minister for Finance, Dr. Swarnim Wagle, to present the Prevention of Money Laundering (Third Amendment) Ordinance, 2083 before the House.
(15:20 hrs.)
Honourable Minister for Finance, Dr. Swarnim Wagle:- Honourable Chairperson, Article 114 (1) of the Constitution of Nepal provides that when the Federal Parliament is not in session, the President may, on the recommendation of the Council of Ministers, issue an ordinance if immediate action is necessary. Similarly, Article 114 (2) states that an ordinance issued under Sub-article (1) shall have the force of law. To further enhance the investigation and prosecution of money laundering related to offenses such as smuggling, customs duty evasion, tax evasion, direct or indirect tax evasion, market manipulation or insider trading in the securities or commodities market, and matters related to currency, banking, finance, foreign exchange, negotiable instruments, and insurance, it has become necessary to immediately amend the existing laws. As both houses of the Federal Parliament are not in session, the Prevention of Money Laundering Ordinance, 2083, which amends the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2064, has been promulgated. Therefore, with the permission of the Honourable Chairperson, I present the Prevention of Money Laundering (Third Amendment) Ordinance, 2083 before the esteemed House. Thank you.
(14:20 hrs.)
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Members, I now provide the floor to the Honourable Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Sobita Gautam, to present the Ordinance to Amend Some Nepal Laws, 2083 before the House.
(15:22 hrs.)
Honourable Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Ms. Sobita Gautam:-
(14:23 hrs.)
Honourable Chairperson, to ensure that state functions are performed promptly and effectively by identifying obstacles in good governance promotion, service delivery, and development construction, it has become necessary to immediately amend the provisions of the existing Nepal laws. Therefore, the Ordinance to Amend Some Nepal Laws, 2083 has been promulgated. This ordinance includes provisions such as amending the Land Act, 2021, to make necessary arrangements for resolving the existing problems of landless Dalits, landless squatters, and unmanaged settlements; amending the Land Revenue Act, 2034, to enable local levels to perform tasks such as registration, name transfer, and cancellation; amending the Forest Act, 2076, to manage forest area usage to remove obstacles encountered during project operation; and to make public service delivery systematic and effective, provisions such as abolishing the trade union related provisions in the Civil Service Act, Health Service Act, and Federal Parliament Secretariat Act, and effectively hearing employee grievances have been included. It has become necessary to make contemporary improvements in various laws related to education, and to make contemporary improvements in 19 laws including the Contribution-based Social Security Act, 2074, the Land Use Act, 2076, the Insurance Act, 2079, and the Law Act, 2081. Therefore, as the Federal Parliament is not in session, with the permission of the Honourable Chairperson, I present the Ordinance to Amend Some Nepal Laws, 2083, promulgated under Article 114 (1) of the Constitution of Nepal, before the esteemed House.
Thank you.
19
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Members, I now provide the floor to the Honourable Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation, Pratibha Rawal, to present the Cooperatives (First Amendment) Ordinance, 2083 before the House.
(14:25 hrs.)
Honourable Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation, Ms. Pratibha Rawal:-
(14:24 hrs.)
Honourable Chairperson, as the Federal Parliament is not in session, it has become necessary to amend certain provisions in the Cooperatives Act, 2074, to bring those who misuse and embezzle cooperative assets under the purview of legal action, to expedite loan recovery and return savings, to regulate and control activities contrary to cooperative principles, to clarify the roles of cooperative registrars and the National Cooperative Regulatory Authority, and to arrange for the licensing of cooperatives primarily engaged in savings and loans through the Authority. To make the regulation, monitoring, and management of the cooperative sector more effective, it has become necessary to amend the cooperative laws immediately. Therefore, with the permission of the Honourable Chairperson, I present the Cooperatives (First Amendment) Ordinance, 2083, promulgated under Article 114 (1) of the Constitution of Nepal, before the esteemed House. Thank you.
Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Members, I now provide the floor to the Honourable Minister for Health and Population, Nisha Mehta, to present the Ordinance to Amend Some Nepal Laws Related to Health Science Institutes, 2083 before the House.
(15:27 hrs.)
Honourable Minister for Health and Population, Ms. Nisha Mehta:- Honourable Chairperson, it is necessary to make Nepal increasingly self-reliant in the health sector, to provide quality health services to citizens, to promote high-level health studies and research, to produce skilled human resources, and to operate established health institutes systematically and effectively. To ensure uniformity in matters such as the tenure and service facilities of office bearers in various health science institutes, and to make service delivery effective by ensuring good governance in the institutes, an ordinance has been promulgated to amend some Nepal laws related to health science institutes. Furthermore, to make the work and activities carried out by health science institutes established and operating for providing easy and quality health services to citizens and for the improvement of the country's health sector more effective and robust, it is necessary to implement legal provisions through an ordinance. Therefore, with the permission of the Honourable Chairperson, I present the Ordinance to Amend Some Nepal Laws Related to Health Science Institutes, 2083 before the esteemed House.
(15:27 hrs.)

I will present it before the Chairperson. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson: - Honorable members, now I provide time to the Honorable Minister of Education, Science and Technology, Sushma Pokharel, to present the bill related to some Nepal Acts concerning Universities, 2083 before the assembly.
Honorable Minister of Education, Science and Technology, Mr. Sushma Pokharel: - Honorable Chairperson, due to the existence of different types of structures according to the prevailing laws related to universities regarding the supreme body of the university, an ordinance, 2083, to amend some Nepal Acts concerning Universities, has been issued to maintain uniformity in the provisions related to such supreme bodies and to make university operations effective and transparent. In order to enhance the political autonomy of universities and remove political interference, and to appoint university officials based on merit, and to further enhance the political autonomy of universities, it is deemed effective to specify the qualifications of the Vice-Chancellor and the Pro-Vice-Chancellor in the Acts related to universities. Considering these matters, and to carry out work accordingly, an ordinance has been issued in accordance with Article 114, Sub-article 1 of the Constitution of Nepal, and amendments have been made to various Acts related to universities. To issue a common law for effective management and operation of universities, as it is necessary to maintain uniformity in the management and operation of universities, it is necessary to implement legal provisions through an ordinance. Therefore, I present the Ordinance, 2083, to amend some Nepal Acts concerning Universities, before the esteemed assembly with the permission of the Honorable Chairperson. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson: - Honorable members, as the Honorable President Ram Chandra Paudel will address a joint meeting of both houses of the Federal Parliament today at 4:00 PM, all honorable members are requested to enter the meeting hall of the House of Representatives by 3:45 PM today and take their seats.
I also request you to be present in the formal attire designated for the honorable members.
The next meeting of the National Assembly will be held today at 5:15 PM, and this meeting is adjourned.
(Thereafter, this meeting was adjourned, and the next meeting will be held today at 5:15 PM.)
Adjourned: 3:30 PM.

sections.name: Opening
sections.summary_en: The first meeting of the 21st session of the National Assembly commenced. The chairperson welcomed the members and read out a letter from the President summoning the session. A moment of silence was observed in tribute to martyrs.

sections.name: President's Address
sections.summary_en: A letter from the President was read, officially summoning the 21st session of the Federal Parliament to convene on Baisakh 28, 2083, at 14:00 hours.

sections.name: Tribute to Martyrs
sections.summary_en: Honorable members observed one minute of silence in remembrance of martyrs who sacrificed their lives for democracy.

sections.name: Chairperson's Address
sections.summary_en: The Chairperson welcomed members to the 21st session, highlighting the continuation of the democratic republic system. The Chairperson acknowledged past contributions, discussed challenges like legislative continuity and building construction, and expressed hope for the new government's performance. The Chairperson also shared experiences from an IPU General Assembly in Istanbul and a conference on adaptive urbanization.

sections.name: Session Agenda and Expectations
sections.summary_en: The Chairperson outlined the agenda for the budget session, including discussions on policy, budget, and key legislation. The introduction of sign language in broadcasts was announced. The Chairperson urged members to prioritize national interests over political differences for the session's success.

speakers.name: Narayan Prasad Dahal
speakers.topic: Session agenda, legislative priorities, call for cooperation

sections.name: Party Representatives' Speeches
sections.summary_en: Honourable Member Kamala Panta of the Nepali Congress spoke, expressing the people's aspirations for stability and development. She criticized the government's style of governance, alleging arbitrariness, misuse of ordinances, and attacks on constitutional bodies and the judiciary. She also raised concerns about state terror and violence against women.

speakers.topic: Criticism of government, constitutional issues, women's rights

sections.name: Opening
sections.summary_en: The session began with a member wishing success for the ongoing session and expressing hope for a proper budget and programs. Another member offered best wishes for the session's success.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Member Jhaku Prasad Subedi criticized the government for circumventing parliament by issuing ordinances, calling it undemocratic and a threat to the rule of law. He highlighted concerns about the Constitutional Council and the appointment of judges. Member Prem Prasad Dangal also criticized the government's use of ordinances, particularly concerning the Constitutional Council and the removal of public office-bearers, and expressed opposition to the eviction of squatters.

sections.name: Adjournment
sections.summary_en: The session concluded with members expressing their views on various issues.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable Member Mahanta Thakur raised concerns about the plight of landless citizens, rising inflation, and the government's actions against professional organizations. He criticized the government's move towards authoritarianism and demanded the repeal of ordinances dissolving student, labor, and civil servant organizations. Honorable Member Tul Prasad Bishwakarma echoed these concerns, highlighting the displacement of landless people, the questionable nature of the ordinances, and the increase in violence against the Dalit community. He urged the government to withdraw the ordinances and take responsible steps to prevent further atrocities.

sections.name: Other Business
sections.summary_en: The Honorable Chairperson announced the receipt of letters from the Office of the President regarding the formation of the Council of Ministers. The letter detailed the appointment, reshuffling, and portfolio allocation of ministers under the leadership of Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, as per the Constitution of Nepal.
